Mr. H. S. CLEMENTS moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 45, to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act. He said: The Bill has a special reference -to the tidal waters of the Pacific coast. If a boom of logs breaks loose, there is no provision made in the present Act whereby anybody may pick up and save the logs. Mr. Speaker, I desire to rise to a question of privilege. I call your attention to an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal on Friday, January 30, 1914, and which reads as follows:
It is current gossip on Parliament Hill to-tlay that Hon. W. S. Fielding, who resigned the editorship of the Montreal Herald-Telegraph yesterday, intends to re-enter the House of Commons at an early day. It is said that Mr. B. B. Law, of Yarmouth, N.S., will resign his seat in his favour. Yarmouth is regarded as a safe Liberal constituency, and there is no <3oubt that the former Finance Minister would
be an immense help to the .Opposition, which is none too effective at present.
I think it is due to my constituents, who have on four different occasions elected me to a seat in this House, and by handsome majorities, to say, in the first place, that there is absolutely no truth in this statement in so far as it refers to myself. 1 have never been asked to resign my seat, nor have I any intention of doing so. 1 propose to stay here and oppose bad legislation whenever it is introduced.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is scarcely to be regarded as a question of privilege, because it does not refer to the hon. gentleman's conduct, nor to his rights and privileges in the House.

The hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) on Friday last asked for certain information with regard to the steamer Alert. This information I have obtained from the responsible officer:
The steamer Alert is employed in the Customs Preventive Service on the Cape Breton coast, and does the work formerly carried on by the steamer Gladiator. The Alert is under the command of Captain Voutier, subject to the general orders of the Chief Preventive Officer of Customs. No instructions were given by the minister, commissioner, or the chief preventive officer regarding the conveyance of Messrs. McLeod and Hayes, as stated in the newspaper clipping read by the member for South Gape Breton. On inquiry I find it has been the practice to carry travellers occasionally on the-Gladiator and the Alert going to remote points where other conveyance was not available, and when not interfering with the regular cruise of the vessel. In order to ascertain the facts regarding the statement read by the member for South Cape Breton, I instructed the chief preventive officer to telegraph to North Sydney. Thp chief preventive officer informs me he received a reply stating that the Alert recently on a trip to Neil's Harbour, took on board as travellers, Joseph McNeill, Phillip McLeod and Dr. Hayes. The member for South Cape Breton is aware that certain parts of the coast are inaccessible except by boat, and if on the occasion in question the Alert was not interfering with her regular cruise, I, personally do not see any reason why any one, even the member for

South Cape Breton himself, should not go on board, and proceed to their destination, should the vessel be going in that direction.

MAGDALEN ISLANDS MAIL SERVICE. Mr. LEMIEUX:
Has the mail contract between Bryan and Leslie, Magdalen Islands, been cancelled? If so, for what reasons?

['The hon. gentleman referred to it for one purpose only, and that was that he wanted to create the impression in Nova Scotia that the Government had plenty of money to give to a service which was not very useful to the country, not nearly so useful as the one he advocated, and the subsidy which he tried to make it appear was not very useful was the subsidy granted to the West Indian steamship line. I am pointing out that this subsidy is of very great value to the fishing industry of Nova Scotia, because I think that I am correct in saying that the bulk of the freight that is carried by the West Indian steamships down to the West Indies is composed of fish caught and cured in Nova Scotia and sent down to the market of the West Indies.
As far as the South African service is concerned, perhaps I might point out that, whereas a few years ago we were sending comparatively small quantities of products to South Africa, owing to the steamship service, I find by the Trade and Navigation returns that last year we sent to South Africa $3,340,513 worth of Canadian products. They went, I think, practically altogether by this subsidized line of steamers, managed by the Elder Dempster Company, and sailing from Montreal in summer and from a Maritime province port in winter to South Africa. The business has been a growing one, and it will continue to grow. This export is made up largely of flour, agricultural implements, newspaper print and other products of Canadian workshops and farms, and that this subsidy is having good results is shown in the development of the trade of Canada and in the opening up of such markets for our manufacturers and producers of other sorts.
The Department of Marine and Fisheries has not -been idle in regard to improvement in the matter of the transportation of fresh fish between the Maritime provinces and the United States. The question has been receiving the consideration of myself and the permanent officers of the department during the past two seasons. By my direction and at my request last year an officer of the department interviewed the officers of the company operating the steamship service between Yarmouth and Boston and arrangements were then made by which the steamship company undertook the more careful and expeditious handling of fresh fish in transit between the Maritime provinces and Boston. Complaints reached the department similar to those made by one hon. gentleman here to-night, complaints that I think were well founded, that lobsters especially were being very carelessly handled, with the result that they reached the Boston market sometimes in a condition which seriously impaired their value. We had the matter investigated. We had an official of the department go down to Boston and be present at the landing of these boats and see the condition in which the fish were, and I am advised by the Deputy M in-ister and other officers in the department that the improvements that have been made have to a very considerable extent been carried out by the steamship companies, that a great deal more care in the handling of fish has been exercised, with the result that fresh lobsters are now in a much more marketable condition when they arrive in the Boston market than they were previously to these inquiries and investigations being made. I am advised by the officials of the department that as a result of the representations made arrangements have been made for more prompt deliveries at Boston on the arrival of the various steamers from Maritime province ports and that better transportation facilities are being provided. At the opening of the present fishing season I directed attention to the matter and requested that the officers of the department should give their consideration to it with the view of bringing about some further improvements. The Superintendent of Fisheries went carefully into the subject, and he has submitted a memorandum pointing out the different steps which should oe taken in order to bring about the desired improvements. These improvements involve negotiations with the Department of Trade and Commerce apd these are in progress at the present time. The steamship', "line which has been referred to as running between Yarmouth and Boston operates one boat from the first of October to the first of June, making two trips a week. After that two boats are put on, which make four trips a week up to the end of July. Then a third boat is put on to the end of October. So that from the first of June to the end of October the service out of Yarmouth is a daily service. There havd been recent negotiations with the company and we hope that a second boat will be placed on the route from October to June instead of one boat as at present. There has been a very large expansion of the shipping business from Yarmouth during recent months and it is to be hoped that with that large expansion of business the steamship company will find that it will be possible to put on a daily service during the months that I have mentioned in order to carry this trade to Boston, and which, as I understand, has been fairly profitable to the company looking at it from a purely business standpoint. The other suggestion, that these boats run along the coast, connecting with the Yarmouth boats, does not find special favour with my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair), who thinks a direct service would be better. But all these questions will have to be considered by the Department of Trade and Commerce.
I think I am absolutely correct in saying that for a period of 15 years, no subsidy has been voted by the Parliament of Canada for a line of steamers running from a Canadian port to a port in the United States, and that is a matter which is worth remembering in connection with this whole question. No subsidy has been given to the line of steamers running from St. John to Portland and Boston, or to the line running from Yarmouth to Boston and return, or from Halifax to Boston and return. However, with the extensive business consequent on the increased development of our fisheries, it would seem to me that the company itself might find it in its own interest, without any subsidy from the Dominion Parliament to put on a line of steamers running daily during the fishing season or during the season when business is most active, between Yarmouth and ports in the United States, as steamers run daily during a great part of the season between St. John and Boston.
I	agree with the hon. member for Guys-borough as to the possibility of developing the fishing industry of Canada. Up to a few years ago Nova Scotia was the premier fish-producing province of Canada. To-day, British Columbia is enormously pro-

ductive. The northern waters of that province are teeming with fish, and although up to the present the industry has been largely developed in only two varieties, the halibut and the salmon, the waters of British Columbia are filled with herring, and sole, and crabs, and other fish, the trade in which can be developed to enormous proportions. With the opening of the Grand Trunk Pacific from Prince Rupert to the East, I believe, from my own personal knowledge and observation in northern British Columbia this year, that in a few years Prince Rupert will not only be the greatest fish port on the continent of America, but probably the greatest fish port in the world. In addition to our fisheries on the eastern and western coasts, we have splendid fisheries in the immense inland lakes, where the industry is capable of great development, with resultant increase in the wealth of the country, and an added source of food supply for the people of the prairie provinces. Owing to the wanton destruction of fish in the past, we will have1 to take measures to repair the mischief that has been done, by providing for file artificial production of the fish. To a very considerable extent, measures in that direction are being taken to-day. This Parliament annually votes a large sum of money for the erection of fish hatcheries and for the maintenance of those already in existence. The Superintendent of Fisheries informs me that for the first time since we have established' fish hatcheries in Canada, they are to-day filled with eggs and are being more successfully operated now than at any time in the past. It has been demonstrated that the salmon hatcheries have done most useful work. The fishermen along the coast of St. John county, who drift out almost across to the Nova Scotia shore night after night in the prosecution of their calling, tell me that there now is no such thing as a year when they are not getting a good supply of salmon. These salmon come up the bay of Fundy, and along the coast making for the spawning grounds on the St. John and Tobique rivers, and they are being caught at points along that river where they were not caught at 15 or 20 years ago, and they are being caught in great numbers. That is a very desirable state of things, and it is due to the more perfect enforcement of the fishery laws, and due most of all to the work of the salmon hatcheries. The same thing is true as to the whitefish hatcheries on the Great Lakes, and although the results obtained from the lobster hatcheries may at the present time

be a matter of some doubt, I trust that in a few years the utility of these hatcheries will be fully demonstrated and that they may in time to come make up for the past depletion of the lobsters fisheries. I entirely agree with one hon. gentleman opposite who said that there has not been as much done for the fisheries of Canada by the Department of Marine and Fisheries as should have been done, but I can assure my hon. friend that the officials of the department to-day are doing their very utmost to promote and develop the fishing industry, and for my part I am giving them the very best assistance and support that it is within my power to give. I trust that in years to come good results will flow from the efforts now being made by the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Now that my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has brought this matter before the House, and has had a full discussion of it, which will no doubt be of benefit, as is every discussion concerning the development of our great national ressouroes, I presume he will consent to the usual course of adjourning the debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Soon after the. disaster which occurred on the Great Lakes in the month of November last, steps were taken to ascertain if it was the intention of the United States, whose shipping had sustained greater loss and damage than Canada's, to appoint any commission of investigation and inquiry, aud it was learned that there was no such intention. The Department of Marine believed that any inquiry, to be effective, should be international in its character; and in view of this, and of the further fact that it was informed that it was the intention of a member of tlie House at the present session to move for a parliamentary committee of inauiry, it was not decided that the appointment of a commission was desirable or necessary.
The following Canadian vessels, which were stranded during the storm on the Great Lakes during the month of November, were the subject of investigation by the Wreck Commissioner:
SS. Turret Chief, owned by the Canadian Lake and Ocean Navigation Co., Ltd., of Montreal; stranded on Keweenaw I'0hit, U.S.A., in lake Superior, at 4 a.m., 8th November, 1913, and still remains there Crew all saved. Formal investigation held November 21 at Kingston. Master censured by court.

SS. Acadian, owned by the Canadian Interlake Line, Limited, Toronto; stranded on shoals near Sulphur island, Thunder bay, U.S.A., in lake Huron, at 4.20 p.m., November 9, 1913. Crew all saved. Towed off November 19, and is now undergoing repairs. Formal investigation held in Toronto, January 30, 1914. Finding not yet rendered.
These two appear to be the only Canadian vessels whose crew's were saved, and direct evidence as to casualty obtainable.

Has the Government received a copy of the following resolution passed on Friday, December 26, 1913, at 8 p.m., by the Executive Board of the Cliambre de Commerce, of Montreal?
Your commission has apprised itself of all that has been said, written and made since twenty years by the Chamber and outside of it on the Georgian Bay canal question, since fifty years, that this question has been before the public, and, after deliberation, it recommends the adoption of the following resolution. It also recommends that copies of this resolution be forwarded to all public bodies, commercial and municipal, in order to obtain their help and adherence, and, thereby, assume the success of energetical, powerful and decisive pressure on the Government.
Whereas, the necessity of the construction of Georgian Bay canal is now so well acknowledged by all, that further arguments in its favour are now useless.
2.	Whereas, the federal Government has already obtained all the necessary information as regards its possibility, its cost and the results which would be brought by the fulfilling of this great national enterprise,
3.	Whereas, the leaders of the different governments at Ottawa have declared themselves in favour of the project
4.	Whereas, at its last session, the Government announced that the canal would not be built until a new commission be appointed to ascertain the commercial results of the scheme, which commission was to make a report at the next session of Parliament
Whereas, the session is now at hand, and this commission has not yet been appointed;
Be it resolved, that the Chambre de Commerce du district de Montreal reiterates with energy its demand on the federal Government for the construction of the Georgian Bay canal within the shortest delay, and assurances of its building at the impending session.
6. That the Chambre de Commerce du district de Montreal protests with all its might against all measures which would entail delay in the realization of this great national project.
Humbly submitted,
A P. Frigon,
President of Special Commission.

' The Prime Minister, therefore, recommends that such an investigation be made forthwith and that the Minister of Customs, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Labour be authorized to instruct the said officials to enter upon such investigation and to co-operate for that purpose, employing and utilizing all information which may be available In the several departments of the Government and obtaining such further data and information as may be necessary or useful for the purposes aforesaid, and that the said officials report upon the matters aforesaid with the least possible delay.

4.	(a). February 28, 1913-date of award. Terms are as follows: (b) Par. 1. Keeping in view the advantage that will accrue to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company in acquiring business for its line of railway from Lake Superior Junction to Fort William and for its system west of Winnipeg from the use of the line between Winnipeg and Lake Superior Junction until the completion of the eastern division, and the advantages that will accrue to the said company in handling its construction material by that channel, and also keeping in view the amount of lake and rail business as compared to all rail business, I award, order and determine that a fair rental for the use of that portion of the eastern division between Winnipeg and Lake Superior Junction, exclusive of the shops at Transcona and repair shops at divisional points until the said eastern division is completed, sufficient for operation within the intent and meaning of the agreements of July 29, 1903, and February 18, 1904, and Acts confirming them which are referred to in the said memorandum of agreement of December 20, 1912, with a ferry at Quebec, is a sum equal to two per cent per annum upon the cost of construction of said portion of the eastern division; the said cost to be ascertained in the manner defined in paragraphs 15 and 16 of said agreement of July 29, 1903, and to include the cost of the items referred to in said paragraphs, but excluding and excepting the cost of construction in like manner of the said shops at Transcona and repair shops at
divisional points and of the lands required or used for said shops. In addition to the said two per cent, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company until the said eastern division is completed as aforesaid, will at its own expense maintain and operate said portion of the eastern division and pay all charges for working expenditure as defined by paragraph 14 of the said agreement of July 29, 1903. Par. 2. With respect to the shops at Transcona, considering their location and the circumstances under which they were produced and furnished, and the specifications and interpreting the said agreements and Acts, in the light ot modern railway practice, and considering the contemplated use of the said eastern division by other railways, I award, order and determine that the said shops are to be regarded as and are a portion of the said eastern division within the intent and' meaning of the said agreements of July 29, 1903, and February 18, 1904, and Acts confirming the same. I further award, order and determine that all repair shops at divisional points are to be regarded as and are a portion of said eastern division within the intent and meaning of said agreements of July 29, 1903, and February 18,	1904,	of the Acts confirming the
same. I consider these are a material part of the railway and necessary for its proper and efficient operation. (Par. 3). In view of my award upon the second question submitted, the third question does not require a finding. (Par. 4.) The capacity and appointment of the Transcona shops are much beyond the needs of the line from Winnipeg to Lake Superior Junction, and no doubt in the interval before completion of the eastern division, and it may be for some time thereafter, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company will avail itself for economic reasons of the use of these shops and outworks to take care of its power, rolling stock, tools and other equipment and materials used upon the line from Lake Superior Junction to Fort William and upon the western division, and upon such other lines or branches as it may construct from the eastern division. I award, order and determine that a fair rental for the use of that portion of the said railway between Winnipeg and Lake Superior Junction, inclusive of the shops at Transcona and repair shops at divisional points, and inclusive of the right of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to use such shops for the purposes of said eastern and: western divisions of said railway, is a sum-

That in the opinion of this House, the question of improved means of transportation for fresh fish between the Maritime provinces and the United States should receive the early attention of the Government.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my purpose in moving this resolution is to interest the Government, if I can, and to induce them to take steps to improve the facilities for the transportation of fresh fish between the Maritime provinces and the markets of the United States. The part of the Maritime provinces in which I am specially interested is possibly the part that most needs those facilities at present, I refer to eastern Nova Scotia. The fishermen are not here asking for any favours. The fishermen, so far as I know, never get any favours, and they do not expect any. The fisherman is accustomed to hard work; he gets up early, he has long hours, and he is exposed to all kinds of weather. If hon. gentlemen, sitting in their cushioned seats in this comfortable Chamber, could see a fisherman in my constituency on one of these January mornings when the thermometer is hovering about zero, ten or twenty miles from land, tossed in his dory on the white caps, attending to his trawls, the spray freezing on his boat and clothing, liable at any minute to encounter a blizzard and be driven out to sea, if hon. gentlemen understood the risk the fisherman endures and the hardships he undergoes in making a living for himself and his family, they would be willing to support any reasonable proposal that would

give him a better price for his products and make his lot somewhat easier.
I need not refer to the importance of our great fishing industry; that will be conceded. By reference to the report laid on the table a few days ago by the Minister of Marine, we find that this industry last year employed 88,308 persons. Of this number, 65,081 were engaged in fishing and 23,327 were workers in canneries and other subsidiary employments connected with fishing. The vessels employed numbered 1,669. The boats engaged numbered 34,501. The market value of the catch last year amounted, according to the report, to $33,389,464. In Nova Scotia the industry has not been expanding of late years. For several years it has simply been marking time and making little or no progress. Last year it actually went back. As a matter of fact, the fishing industry in the Maritime provinces has never had a fair chance. It has been carried on under very great disadvantages, the chief of these being the distance from the market and the lack of transportation facilities. Up to a few months ago we were shut out of the market of the United States by a heavy tariff, and for many years we were practically shut out of the markets of Montreal, Toronto and the Canadian cities by the distance we were from them and the heavy express charges. Of late years this has been partly overcome. The Department of Marine and Fisheries is assisting in the transportation of fish in Canada, and doing so with excellent re- , suits. This assistance commenced under the late Administration in the year 1909, and it has been continued by the present Administration. Prior to this, the express rate from Mulgrave and Haliiax to Montreal was $1.50 per hundred pounds. At the same time the rate from Portland and Boston to Montreal was about 80 cents. You can see that this was a very heavy handicap on the fishermen of the Maritime provinces. In 1909, under the Administration of the late Government, an agreement was made with the railways and the express companies that has been of immense advantage to the trade in the Maritime provinces. The terms of this agreement between the Government and the express companies were: The department arranged to have the railway place at the disposal of the shippers a cold storage car on two days each week, which car would be hauled by fast freight to Montreal. To enable this to be done, the department guaranteed that the earnings on these cars would be at
least two-thirds those on a minimum carload of 20,000 pounds, at carload lot rates from the point of starting to destination, plus $4 per car for icing. The department arranged with the express companies to accept responsibility for one-third of the ordinary express rates on all shipments of fresh and mildly cured fish, including shell fish, from the Atlantic coast as far west as the eastern boundary of Manitoba, and from the Pacific coast as far east as the said boundary. This service has proved a great boon to the trade. While it cost the department a considerable amount annually for the first few years, it is now being taken advantage of to such an extent that it is practically self-sustaining. In this way we have developed a good home market for fresh fish caught in the Maritime provinces. But a new situation has arisen owing to the Wilson tariff, which has opened up to the people of the Maritime provinces the great market of the United States. We have only to look at the map of the Maritime provinces to see the proximity to the New England States, with their teeming population, and cheap water carriage and open navigation the whole year round. If our fisheries are ever to become a great industry, we must exploit this market in the United States. The Boston market, in addition to its proximity to the Maritime provinces, has the advantage of being a much larger market than anything we have in Canada. I am told by dealers who have experience in the fishing business that if two or three carloads were sent to Montreal for sale on the same day it would practically break the market, but you could put three or four times that amount on the Boston market and it would have no such effect, because Boston is such a large distributing centre. The ruling prices in Boston are also much higher than the prices in the Maritime provinces. This is shown very clearly by comparing the prices quoted from day to day on the Boston market with the prices that the fishermen are receiving on the coast of my own constituency.

How do the Boston
prices compare with Montreal prices?

I am discussing the
price the fisherman receives for his fish at the place where it is caught. The retail prices in Montreal, Ottawa and other Canadian cities, have always been a puzzle to me; they are so much higher than we should expect them to be. For instance a fisherman in the town of Canso gets one

and a half cents a pound for the haddock he catches at this season of the year, but you cannot buy the same pound of haddock in Ottawa for less than ten cents. That is a matter I am not able to explain. I am talking in the interests of the producer and am pointing out that the prices paid in Boston to the man who catches the fish are very much higher than the prices paid to the man who catches the fish in the province of Nova Scotia. If you look at the trade papers of the first of January, you will find that the price in Boston was $5.50 per 100 pounds of haddock while the price at Canso was only $1.50. I have a report before me-not a very recent one-taken from the Gloucester Daily Times of February 6, 1913, nearly a year ago, which illustrates the point I am making. At that time haddock was selling wholesale in Boston for $6 per 100 pounds and on certain days the price was higher, from $8 to $10 per 100 pounds. On the 7th February- quoting from the same paper-the fisherman got for his haddock landed at the wharf in Boston from $4 to $8 per 100 pounds, and for large cod from $8 to $9 per 100 pounds. Although the price varies very much in Boston it is as a rule very much higher than the price ruling in Nova Scotia. I have a third quotation from the same paper-which is the best authority we have on this question-dated the 18th of February, which shows that Boston dealers were paying $4 to $5.50 per 100 lbs. for haddock and $6 for large cod.' During all this period the fisherman at Canso was getting $1.50 for the same class of fish. As I have pointed out, this Boston market with its higher prices is open to us and the question is: have we the enterprise and the pluck to take advantage of our opportunity? Whatever views some of our people may have held about this matter during the hysterical period of 1911, there are, to-day, very few business men in the province of Nova Scotia who do not recognize that it would be a great advantage to the fishing industry of that province to have the United States market open to us. I do not think there are two opinions about that among the business men of our province to-day. I will give you the opinion of Mr. S. Y. Wilson, a prominent fish dealer who has spent all his life in the trade, and who should know as much as anybody in the constituency of Halifax, about this matter. He is also a prominent supporter of the Prime Minister. He says:
Clear-cut evidence of what 'free fish' is doing for the Nova Scotia fisherman is seen in the 
preparations taking place aboard schooners at the ports of La Havre and Lunenburg. These preparations mean that Nova Scotians are going to cut out the Gloucester men in the operation of the winter herring industry at Newfoundland. Right now even have they begun to elbow the Gloucester fleet from a fishery it has controlled for years, several craft having set out to secure cargoes.
All this has been made possible by the recent enactment of the Underwood tariff schedule, abolishing the import tax on sea food irrespective of the transportating ship's nationality.
Another prominent man, Mr. A. Hand-field Whitman of Halifax, in discussing this question in the New Year's issue of the Morning Chronicle, newspaper, siays:
The outstanding incident in 1913 in regard to the fishing industry was the removal of the duty by the United States Government. Free entry of fish into the United States must bring a tremendous development in Canada's fishing industry.
Everybody who has read the reciprocity agreement knows that it would have given us much greater benefits than we enjoy under the Wilson tariff. The reciprocity agreement would have given us practically a monopoly of the United States market, while the fisherman from abroad who shipped his salt mackerel to the United States from England, Ireland or Holland, would have to pay $2 a barrel, Canadian mackerel, under the reciprocity agreement, would have entered the United States market free of duty. The Wilson tariff does not give us that advantage because we have to compete with other nations in the American market.
The chief difficulty in taking advantage of the United States market is the want of transportation facilities. Our needs in Eastern Nova Scotia, and I am speaking now largely for my own constitutency, are twofold; in the first place, we require a branch railway in order to reach our home market, and our home market of course is not to be despised. At present we look upon it as the best market we have, and it will continue to develop as the population of the country increases. But in the constituency that I have the honour to represent we are not able to get into touch with the home market owing to the lack of railway facilities. Apart from my own constituency, and speaking for the southern coast of Nova Scotia generally, I am of opinion that a fast line of boats connecting our chief ports with the city of Boston would be of immense advantage to the fishing industry and would help to develop a very large trade with the United States. I have brought this question of branch lines to the attention of my hon. friend the Minister

of Railways and Canals several times. He has given me various answers and does not seem to be in any great hurry to deal with this question. At all events he cannot be charged with any indecent haste in regard to it. But he has been talking about it for several years. In 1912, when I asked him if he was prepared to go forward with the proposition which was inaugurated by the late Government, he informed me that he would require to have a survey made before he could say that. In 1913 he informed me that he would require to send a traffic expert down to see that country in order to find out whether the Government would be justified in spending any money on that branch line. To-day he tells me that the matter is under consideration. I do not know what has happened or what is going to be done, but it is always something in the future; it is like the little boy's complaint about his mother; it is jam to-morrow, jam the day after to-morrow, but it is never jam to-day. I would like to have this question brought to a head and have the minister deal with it. Any one who has followed the discussion in the House will remember that the late Government undertook to build certain branch lines in the province of Nova Scotia and one through this territory, and that a contract was let for the building of this line prior to the defeat of the late Government. A deposit of $50,000 was put up by the contractor, and the Sunnybrae branch was purchased from the Nova Scotia Steel Company at a cost of $100,000 to form part of the line. All of these things were done at the time this Government came into power. The same situation existed with regard to the branch line in the county of Halifax. The branch line in the county of Halifax went on and I am told that it will be completed next summer. But, the contract was cancelled in the county of Guysborough, the $50,000 deposit was paid back to the contractor and ever since that day we have been having evasive answers from the Government as to what they intend to do in reference to this branch line.
I pointed out to the minister last year that if he did undertake to build this branch line he would find sufficient traffic to justify the expenditure; that a large tourist traffic could be developed, and that along the proposed line, there are large quantities of spruce and hardwood and also quantities of pulp and pitwood for which there is a good market in the coal mines of Gape Breton. The railway would also
pass through a good agricultural country, but perhaps the greatest development would take place in connection with our fishing industry. That is what I am dealing with chiefly to-night. As a proof of the position I take in connection with the fishing industry, I would like to place before the House some statistics as to what has been done at Canso, Queensport, Half Island Cove, and places around Chedabucto bay that are now brought into connection with the railway at Poit Mulgrave by a steamboat service. speechtext: Does my hon. friend mean three trips a week between the Maritime provinces and Boston, or does he mean three trips a week between Yarmouth and Boston?

I am not speaking just now for Yarmouth, because Yarmouth has pretty good facilities. I presume the hon. member for Yarmouth will tell us what is being done at that point. I am chiefly concerned now with eastern Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I wanted to understand it my hon. friend is advocating that a direct line of steamers should be put on between Canso and the ports to which he refers, and Boston; or, that there should be a line of steamers from these ports to Yarmouth to connect with the steamers from Yarmouth to Boston.

I would have no objection to the system being combined with the present line of steamers. I am not undertaking to say how it ought to be done. If I can persuade the Government to give us steamboat communication between these ports and Boston, the Government will have to work out the details as to how it is best to do it. I do not want to duplicate the boats from Yarmouth to Boston, but I presume the Government would not do that unless they thought it absolutely necessary to do so. My own view is that a successful business can best be done by freight boats. The boats from Boston to Yarmouth are passenger boats. I would like to see a fast fish line in the business that would be devoted specially to carrying fish, and I do not know whether it would be wise that passengers should be included. As I have stated, this will involve the expenditure of a considerable sum of money, but in my judgment it would be justified. It would bring much better results than some of the expenditures we are now making. For instance, we are asked to vote the large sum of $340,666 to assist steam service between Canada and the West Indies and South America, and we are also asked to vote $146,000 for steam service with South Africa. I am not objecting to these subsidies, but I do say that if you could give us one-half of these sums to equip a fish-carrying service between our Atlantic ports and the American market, you will get far better results than
you will ever get out of the South American trade or out of the South African trade.
I regard this as the chance of a lifetime for the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He does not need to travel like Gulliver all over the world to find this trade; it is right at his very door staring him in the face. Look at it; we have teeming millions of people across the boundary, and they are a fish-consuming people. They must get their chief supply from Canada, either from the Pacific coast or from the Atlantic coast. We have in eastern Canada five thousand miles of coast line comprising perhaps the most valuable fisheries in the world. We have the men. There are no better men on the seven seas than there are in eastern Canada. We have the harbours; we control the bait and we control the base of supplies. In addition to all this, the richest, the biggest and the best market in the world is thrown open to us. What we have not got and never have had is proper transportation facilities. That is what we are asking for.
I regard this as a real emergency. The question will arise: will this Government take advantage of the splendid opening for which the people of Nova Scotia have been waiting and looking for the last fifty years? It is quite true that by taking advantage of this opening, there will be more truck and trade with the Yankees, but we have that now on a very large scale and it is growing larger year by year. On this question of trade with the Yankees we have an extraordinary situation in this country. If we are to adopt the Tory philosophy of 1911, that it would endanger British connection, we have at the present time our Canadian patriotism flowing across the boundary line at the rate of $2,000,000 a day for every day of ten hours during the whole of 1913. That is $200,000 an hour or $3,333.33 every minute. This is an alarming state of affairs. The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White) however does not appear to be taking any steps to stop it. He just sits in his cozy seat, shuts one eye and winks at the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid), and both gentlemen are laughing in their sleeves at the poor deluded devils who left our party and voted Tory in 1911, for the purpose of stopping this trade with the Yankees.
I hope that no considerations of consistency will deter the Government from taking steps in regard to the matter that I am proposing. A great American philosopher once said that consistency was the hobgoblin of little minds. Speak what you think to-day in words as hard as cannon balls.

and to-morrow speak again what you think in words as hard again, although you should contradict every word that you said to-day. That is the philosophy I would commend to my hon. friends on the other side, owing to the circumstances in which they find themselves.
My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) would have to turn a sharp corner in order to do this, but he turned a sharp corner not long ago on the naval question and I think he is quite capable of doing so again. I hope that he will deal with the situation promptly and vigorously, and that he will do whatever is necessary to put the project on its feet. I venture to say that it will be the greatest stroke of business that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce will ever have an opportunity of doing for the Maritime provinces. Let him do this and great results will follow. Towns will grow up all along our coasts. Our deserted shipyards will spring into life again. Thousands of our best seamen, who are now the hirelings of the nabobs of Boston and Gloucester, will return home to develop our own country; the Maritime provinces will win back their old prestige on the sea and Canada will take her rightful place as a great Maritime power. Is not that an achievement worthy of a statesman, even if he has to turn a sharp corner in order to carry it out ? I hope that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce will measure up to the opportunity and that, when the Supplementary Estimates are tabled, he will be able to find a favourable solution.

The people of the Maritime provinces have already benefited very considerably by the action of the United States Government in

putting fish upon the free list. What my hon. friend from Guysborough suggests is quite within the means and power of the present Government. We have a line of steamships running between the town of Port Hawkesbury and the city of Boston which are already operated during the summer months. Unfortunately, the owners of these boats, not being in the enjoyment of any subvention from the federal Government, do not feel any special obligation to develop the business except that which comes to them in the ordinary way. While these steamships take their departure from Port Hawkesbury, in Inverness county, they make no call along the coast of Nova Scotia until they come to Halifax, and from Halifax they sail direct to Boston. It would be a very desirable and commendable object if the Government would adopt a system which would induce, if not the present steamship company plying from Port Hawkesbury and Halifax to Boston, then some other steamship company, to place steamers on that route that would call not only at Port Hawkesbury but also call at Arichat and take the fish week by week that would offer for transportation along that route. The county I have the honour to represent is about in the same position as Guysborough as regards the incompleteness of its railway accommodation. We have a railway from Point Tupper to St. Peters. But it is a privately-owned road, and so, unfortunately, a shipment of fish sent over it by express must pay a double rate before reaching its destination. The acquisition of the Cape Breton railway by the Government, the extending of it to Arichat and Sydney and Louisburg, and its operation as a branch of the Intercolonial railway, would be a boon that I have endeavoured to urge upon the Government in the past. I reiterate the desirability of this project, and I hope that the plan for the acquiring o! these branch lines as feeders for the Intercolonial railway has not been abandoned, notwithstanding the fact that no intimation has been given by His Royal Highness at the opening of Parliament that would lead us to believe that the present Government intends taking up that question in the very near future. The present transportation is entirely inadequate for the people of the province of Nova Scotia as respects the important industry to which I refer. I desire to impress upon the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries as well the absolute necessity of accepting the principle embodied in the resolution moved by the hon. member for
Guysborough and voting at an early day a sum of money to assist the transportation problems of Nova Scotia in the shipment of fresh and salt fish to Boston in the same manner as that in which they have dealt with the transportation between Victoria and the city of San Francisco.

The resolution brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), to my mind, embodies one of the most important questions that this House has been called on to consider. Representing as I do the county of Yarmouth, which is the gateway between Nova Scotia and the United States, I should not be doing my duty if I did not say a word in connection with this subject. The hon. member for Guysborough has dealt with the matter in a very large and broad manner; I propose, in the few minutes which I intend to occupy, to deal with it more from a local standpoint. We have had from the port of Yarmouth for sixty years, owing to the energy and enterprise of the people of
Yarmouth, a steamboat service
9 p.m. between Yarmouth and Boston.
For many years these boats were owned by the people of Yarmouth, down to the time when the Dominion Atlantic railway absorbed the old Yarmouth Steamship Company. Afterwards this was taken over by the Canadian Pacific railway, and lately the Canadian Pacific railway has transferred the boats and steamboat sec vice to the Boston and Yarmouth Steamboat Company. Twenty or twenty-five years ago we had two ships per week from Yarmouth to Boston. We have the same to-day. But I am happy to say that the steamboat service is, at the present time, and since the coming into effect of the Wilson tariff in October last, has been inadequate to carry the fresh fish and other goods that are offered for transportation from Yarmouth to Boston. As I have said, Yarmouth is the gateway to and from the western part of Nova Scotia. There is no steamboat communication between the Maritime provinces and Boston short of St. John on the north and Halifax on the east. And in many instances fish has been sent direct from Halifax by train to connect with the boats from Yarmouth to Boston. The people of Yarmouth realized the truth of what we said when we told them, weeks and weeks before September, 1911, that to give the fishermen of the Maritime provinces entry for their fresh fish into the United States

market would bring about an era of development such as they bad never seen before. And the present state of affairs proves the truth of what we said at that time. I am glad to say that the people of Yarmouth were not hoodwinked by the excuses and arguments used by our friends on the opposite side when they said that we did not want the United States market, that the United States were composed of ninety millions of hogs and we wanted no dealings with them. I can only say that if the people of the United States are hogs, we like to deal with them. The money we get from them is clean, and it is about the only money we do get. I do not wish to speak in an offensive manner, but every dollar we get from the sale of fish to the United States we have to spend to pay for flour, feed, harness and almost everything else we use. There is nothing we can ship to Ontario, but our trade is naturally with the United States. Since the Wilson tariff came into effect there has not been a trip of these steamers when they have not been obliged to leave freight behind. I desire to read a letter which appeared in the Yarmouth Herald of the 27th of January last, which deals with the question of transportation :
Dear Sir,-Kindly allow us a short space in your valuable columns for a few remarks concerning our transportation facilities. It comes to this: Something must be done in order to make provision to have more accommodation for carrying the freight from Yarmouth to Boston.
There has not been a single trip this season that all the freight has been taken to Boston, and in a few instances there has been almost a load for the boat left on the wharf and at other stations.
Now there is one sure remedy for this, and that is to get a line of boats in opposition. Already there is a petition afloat, and is being freely signed by the shippers of all kinds of fresh and salt fish in the different localities.
Hoping that this will meet with the approval of all concerned, and thanking you, Mr. Editor, for your valuable space, we are,
Yours truly,
Shippers.
I must say I do not quite agree with the third paragraph of that letter, that the only sure remedy is in an opposition boat. I am afraid that if another boat were put on that route, we should have a very poor service indeed. I think that the proposals which I intend to make to the Government before I conclude would be very much better.
