On the two trips she carried fish and fish products to the value of $59,000 and she left behind on the wharf at Yarmouth quite a quantity of fish which she could not carry. Something, of course, must be done. The fishermen of the province of Nova Scotia and of Canada have had very little done for them. I do not know of any means of helping them except the proposals I intend to make. They are engaged in one of the most hazardous occupations I know of. They are exposed to danger and storm and hardly a week passes without the loss by drowning of one. two, three or more of these fishermen. The boats which they use to prosecute their business are small gasoline boats and they are anxious, of course, to get off to their lobster traps in the winter; and on that coast it is no pleasure trip to go on the sea at any time during the winter season. These fishermen have not had very much done for them. I was in hopes that the people of Canada, when they had an opportunity of voting in September last, would have voted for reciprocity which would have given the greatest era of prosperity that Canada has ever seen. We are getting some of the benefits of it to-day, but of course only to a small extent. Where the Boston is making two trips a week to-day, I am positive that inside of two months they will have to make four trips a week. The Board of Trade have taken this matter up with the Steamship Company, and I understand that they have promised four trips before the first of March. I think that under the circumstances this Government should do something for the fishermen. They were promised many things in the campaign of 1911, and I am sure that the member for Queens and Shelburne (Mr. 

McCurdy) will remember many of these promises. The argument was used that a lot was to be done for the fishermen if this Government eame into power. They went iso far as to say that the fishermen of Nova Scotia would be provided with medicine free. If they wanted a box of pills or a dose of salts or anything this Government was prepared to furnish it to them; but I am sorry to say that up to the present these fishermen have suffered, I presume, untold miseries from the lack of these medicines which were promised them. I desire to say that my idea of assisting the fishermen of the western part of Nova Scotia is by the installation of cold storage on board the steamers plying between Yarmouth and Boston. The lobster, as many of you know, has to be marketed alive and is different from most any other fish. A lobster arriving in Boston dead or, as they call it, sleeping, is immediately thrown away as unfit for use. On the boats between Yarmouth and Boston there are not proper facilities for handling this fish or landing [DOT]them without much loss. By the installation of cold storage a large amount of money would be saved for the fishermen, and I believe the Government should assist the ^steamboat company in providing cold storage on board these steamers for the better facility of handling not only lobsters but -other fish which is sent to Boston.
The second point I would urge upon the Government to-day to assist the fishermen in marketing their fish would be to improve the harbour accommodation. The managers [DOT]of the Boston and Yarmouth Steamship ,Company tell me that to put another boat on the route between Yarmouth and Boston involves a very large amount of money, and, having handled ships for some years, I am quite *confident that they are right in this *statement. Larger boats could be built and run between these two ports and the service could be increased. My own opinion lis that with free entry of fish into the United States market it will not be long before two boats are required.
The third suggestion I have to make to the Government is that in order to improve the facilities between Yarmouth and Boston dredging rshould be done and our harbour should be improved. The boats which are running there to-day, making two trips per week in winter and six trips in summer, [DOT]are as large as the port of Yarmouth will accommodate, and I sincerely hope that the Government may see fit, instead of putting a large amount 25
of money in the Estimates, as they have done during the time they have been in power, and not spending it, will put a large amount in the Estimates and spend it. Our port at Yarmouth is one of the most important on the coast. It serves the counties of Digby and Annapolis, and it serves the whole south shore, all the way to Halifax. It is the port for the transportation, not only of fish, but of all other articles of produce, and I trust that the Government will see its way clear to give a large appropriation for improving and dredging the harbour of Yarmouth so that larger boats can be put on the route and that transportation companies will not have the excuse that there is not water enough in Yarmouth harbour to put on large boats. Let us put the horse before the cart and not the cart before the horse, let us not wait until the boats are ready to come and then find that there is not enough water for them to enter the harbour. Let us do the dredging first and invite the transportation companies to put on larger boats and give our fishermen and farmers proper transportation facilities, which they must have between the western part of Nova Scotia and Boston. The western part of Nova Scotia has dealt with Boston for many, many years. To-day, with the duty off fish and with the duty off our produce to a certain extent, although nothing like the same extent as it would have been under the reciprocity agreement, a trade will spring up between those ports which the boats at present on the route will be quite unable to handle.

I would like to make a suggestion to the Government in regard to this matter, which I think would be of advantage to the people of the western part of Canada and of Ontario. Instead of subsidizing steamers to carry this beautiful fish from [DOT]the Maritime provinces to the United States, I would suggest that the Government provide transportation facilities in connection with the Intercolonial railway so that the people of Ontario, Manitoba and the West can get the benefit of the fish taken from the eastern waters of Canada. A great number of people are engaged in the Maritime provinces to-day in fishing. The cost of transporting this fish to Ontario is very great and I think the Government instead of subsidizing steamers as suggested by the hon. gentlemen opposite, should reduce freight rates between the Maritime provinces and the West, there-



by giving western people the benefit of this fish. To-day if the people of Ontario want fish they have to get it from Portland. The United States provides facilities for shipping this fish from Portland, and why should not our own railways be utilized for distributing this fish throughout Canada? In the province from which I come, a great quantity of fish is caught, especially on the north side, but unfortunately we have no railway facilities to take that fish from the north side to the main line of the Prince Edward Island railway, but I think that within a very short time the Government will see fit to provide such facilities. I have no doubt that when the oar ferry from Prince Edward Island to the mainland is built a great impetus will be given to the fish industry, and then the people of western Canada, and especially Ontario -we in the East call Ontario West-will receive the benefit of this fish. I know the Minister of Railways is inclined if a sufficient inducement is held out, to put on fish trains from Hawkesbury and Halifax to Montreal, and I should think that these men who have been shouting for a subsidy for steamers from Yarmouth and Hawkesbury would see that it would be in their interests to work up a trade within their own country.

I
desire to place myself on record as supporting the resolution of my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair). I have listened with considerable interest to what my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. McLean) has said. He would intimate that the late Government did not do very much for the fish trade upon the Atlantic coast. I am of the opinion that the late Government did a great deal in that direction. My hon. friend must not forget that the late Government made certain arrangements by which cold storage cars from Atlantic ports to Montreal were placed at the disposal of eastern shippers on two days in the week and were to be hauled by fast freight. Not only that, but the late Government guaranteed the payment of one-third of the express rates from Mulgrave and Halifax to the eastern boundary of Manitoba. I think similar concessions were given to the western part of the country. My hon. friend should not forget these facts. I am quite in agreement with him that anything that can be done to help along the trade between the East and the centre and West of Canada, is an excel-

lent idea, and I would always be in favour of that. But we in the East are ambitious; we are not satisfied with one market-If there is another market offering-and a good market we know it is-have we not a perfect right to look for it? If there are a dozen markets offering I think we should try to get them. In my opinion, that is what constitutes a great nation. However, my hon. friend will not forget after this, to give credit where credit is due. I must thank my hon. friend from Guysborough for bringing up this matter in the House. I must also congratulate him and other hon. gentlemen for having given us so much information. I cannot hope in the short time at my disposal to contribute very much to this discussion. I wish, however, to refer to the fish trade as it affects my own county. The fish trade in eastern Canada previous to 1907 was at a low ebb and in anything but a satisfactory condition, and remained so until the concessions I referred to were made by the late Government. Ever since then, the trade of Montreal, Toronto and western Canada has been increasing in a very satisfactory way. That trade was formerly in the hands of our American neighbours, but we succeeded in capturing it from them, and it is now a great boon to our eastern shippers.
I desire to refer to a return I received this afternoon with regard to the Fishery Advisory Board, which to my mind is an institution calculated to greatly benefit the industry. I am sorry however, and I want to call the attention of my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. A. A. McLean) to this, that there is not a man on that Advisory Board east of the city of Halifax. That is unfortunate, because our best fishing grounds are around the Island of Cape Breton and off the coast of Guysborough County and our biggest fish shipping ports are around the coast of the county of Guysborough and in Cape Breton Island particularly Port Hawkesbury, Port Hood. and Margaree, Grand Etang and Cheticamp. There is another defect in this board-a very serious defect to my mind-and that is the absence of real fishermen. There are eighteen members on the board and with the exception of one, I think, they are all business men. I regard that as a great mistake. I consider that one-half of the members of that board should be men engaged in the fishing industry. I take it that the duty of the board is to inform the Government as to what the fishing industry and trade really requires, and I wish to call the attention of

my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to that. Possibly he may revise the list. This Advisory Board could be of great help to the fishing industry, but I fear that industry will not receive the attention from the board that it would receive if we had, at least, a sprinkling of fishermen on it.
Just a word or two with regard to the American market which has been thrown open to us by the Underwood tariff. Some hon. gentlemen opposite will tell us that the Underwood tariff has opened up the markets of the United States to us and that we will get the same measure of benefit from it as we would have from reciprocity.
I do not believe that it would do this at all. The fact is we had the exclusive trade privileges under reciprocity whereas under the present American tariff we must share that privilege with all the nations of the world. I took the trouble to look up the shipments from other countries to the United States. We have competitors today in the American market with some of the mist aggressive traders in the warld in fish and fish products. We must compete particularly with three countries-Norway, Newfoundland and the United Kingdom. Of the very articles of fish that are shipped from our country into the United States, I might say that the United Kingdom sends nearly $2,000,000 worth to that country. We are in competition with Newfoundland which sends in a million dollars worth of the very same class of article of fish. We are in competition with Norway which sends a million and a half dollars worth of the same kind of fish to the United States. Under the reciprocity agreement we had an exclusive right, which we cannot hope to enjoy under the Underwood tariff. That is one reason why I believe we should get as much aid from the Government as we possibly can to enable us to cope successfully with those countries. I trust that the resolution moved by my hon. friend from Guysborough will fall upon fertile soil. I trust that it will be productive of some good result and that our means of transportation to that country will receive honest and careful consideration from this Governement.
I am particularly anxious for the reason, I suppose, that I represent here a constituency that is more in need of the improved transportation facilities for fish than any other constituency in Canada. We have one of the finest fishing counties in Canada, we 25 i	.	.
have a hundred miles of coast along the county of Inverness, fronted by the finest fishing grounds in the world, but unfortunately. we are deprived of good harbours. They are all bar harbours along that coast. We are also bound up for four or five months of the year with ice. This makes it very difficult to carry on the fishing industry as we would like to carry it on because the-industry can be carried on along this particular coast to a marvelously greater degree that it has been in the past if we can only get improved facilities for transporting our fish to the American market. I may say, as my hon. friend from Yarmouth (Mr. Law) has already said, that it is an unfortunate thing that our harbours have been neglected so very much for the last two and a half years. I am not going to refer to this particularly now as I hope to have another opportunity later on to discuss several cases in detail.
When the late Government went out of office there was at least $200,000 of public grants to be spent along that coast. Not one dollar of that money has been spent, but the saddest thing of all is that our harbours, wharfs and breakwaters along the coast are in a deplorable condition. I can say without the slightest exaggeration that at least $100,000 worth of public property along the coast of Inverness was destroyed within the last two years when an expenditure of not more than $3,000 would have save this property. The money was granted but it was never spent there. It is most unfortunate, but it is true. That is the situation we are in. We have noproper harbours and we are tied up by ice for a large section of the year.
There is only one way by which we can hope to develop our fisheries along that coast and that is by the construction of a line of railway from Orangedale on the Intercolonial to Cheticamp. I have advocated the construction of this road since I have had the honour of a seat in this House. Before the late Government went out of office I had the assurance-and I make the statement in the presence of hon. gentlemen who were members of that Government- that this line would be constructed and I am convinced had the late Government been returned to power this road would be nearing completion now. Further than that, I called the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) to it. I intend to go more into detail in connection with the construction of this proposed road later on.

I was very much pleased to hear the statement of the hon. member for Yarmouth (Mr. Law) that the steamship company which operates between Yarmouth and Boston, had given an assurance to the Yarmouth Board of Trade that they would, on March 1, put extra boats on that service to give the much desired four trips a week. It has always been somewhat of a puzzle to me why, with such a large quantity of freight-and valuable freight at that-offering at Yarmouth, the steamship company which ' undertakes to look after that business should not of their own volition supply sufficient boats to take care of the traffic which is pressing on them.
It goes without saying that every one interested in the development of the fishing industry along the southern shore ,of Nova Scotia, and I am keenly concerned in this matter, is interested in any proposition which makes for better transportation facilities for our fish to all points on which we depend for our market.
I would be the last to fail to appreciate the assistance given by the late Government towards improving transportation facilities and the safe and rapid despatch of fish and fish products to the markets. I believe that the assistance given by way of a rebate on express charges on fresh fish shipments did much towards facilitating the movement of fresh fish to the western market, but I would remind hon. gentlemen opposite that the present Government has already taken another and very important step in advance in that direction. We must all know that in order to land fish fresh on the market, we require not iced express shipments or a refrigerator freight car service, but an express refrigerator car service .
The efforts of the late Government were devoted towards shipments by express which embraced ordinary package shipment and iced shipment; the latter was not effective, because the ice often melted before the fish had travelled 100 miles on their journey, and the fish being placed on the market in poor condition made a poor advertisement for the Canadian fishing industry.
To afford further facilities and to place the trade on a better footing, the present Government has made arrangements by which regular express refrigerator service is
available, and that is a most decided advantage to the industry.
It was with surprise that I heard such an astute gentleman as the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) refer to what he described as the ' hysterical campaign ' against reciprocity.
I may say that when the reciprocity campaign was launched, I had no hesitation in leaving a quiet business life and most pleasant surroundings to do what I regarded was my duty, in opposing what I then considered a * bad bargain', and I claim that subsequent developments in connection with the fishing industry and the changes which the Americans have voluntarily made in their tariff on fish, amongst other of our natural products which they purely in their own interests made, have vindicated the stand taken by the Conservative party on the reciprocity question.
The hon. member for Guysborough has admitted the value of the home market. He probably knows, as well as any of us, that prior to the time when a duty was placed on finnan haddies, bloaters, kippers and other mild-cured or cured fish, our supply for consumption in Canada came from Gloucester, Portland and Boston. He knows well that the placing of a duty on such fish, and the assistance given by way of a rebate on express charges, built up in western Canada a valuable market for Canadian fish of that class. He knows that that market is now supplied, not from Boston, Gloucester, and Portland, but from Lockeport, Digby, Halifax, Canso and other places in eastern Canada. The hon. member (Mr. Sinclair) has to-night admitted the value of that market, and he has even gone so far as to say that he considers it our best market. When the reciprocity pact was put forward, we were in effect asked insofar as the Canadian market was concerned, to revert to conditions which existed in the old days when the Canadian market for this fish was supplied from Boston, Portland and Gloucester. We were asked to admit the American fish free into the Canadian market, which, as the hon. member for Guysborough says, is our best market, and we in turn were to have our fish admitted into the Boston market, which altho a broad, is an erratic market. I repeat that the policy1 of the Conservative party with regard to reciprocity has been vindicated because we have got without cost to us as valuable concessions from the United States as we would have obtained had the reciprocity pact been confirmed by the electors and our home markets sacrificed.

Our fish is now being admitted free into the American market, whatever that is worth, and it is worth something, I admit, and we have, at the same time., retained our home market. I cannot but think that the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), in his heart of hearts, knows that we are better off to-day than if his fiscal theories had been approved of in 1911 by the Canadian electors. The hon. gentleman is a man of shrewdness who can appreciate a good bargain when he sees it, and I am quite sure that the view which I have put forward will appeal to his good business judgment.
Of course, every hon. member of ""the House approves of the idea contained in the resolution: that so far as legitimate assistance can be given to encourage the fishing industry it should be given. But when we come down to ways and means hon. gentlemen opposite are as diverse in their recommendations and differ as much in their ideas as to how actually the industry can be assisted, as they differ in regard to their selection of a new trade policy. They talk of subsidizing numerous and diverse steamship routes. There is one thing that occurs to me in connection with this discussion, and it is, that although these gentlemen opposite were in power for fifteen years, if I am correctly *informed, they never initiated a precedent by subsidizing one single steamship line to develop trade between ^Canada and the United States. Fifteen years was surely long enough for them to decide upon some action, and be it Temembered that their inaction was during a period when owing to more unfavourable conditions in the fishing industry, assistance was more required than under the conditions which exist to-day.
Being in somewhat constant touch with the Department of Marine and Fisheries, I am very phased to note the great interest which the minister at the head of the department takes in the improvement of the administration of his department and the improvement of the many services connected with it.
In that regard, reference has been made to-night to the appointment of the Fisheries Advisory Board. A Shell-fish Commission has also been appointed. Accurate knowledge must precede action, and the hon. minister has been active in order to get the best suggestions possible as to what should be done in regard to the improve-

*merit of this industry. Those who are as closely in touch with the fishing industry as I have had the good fortune of being, cannot have failed to note the improvement in the enforcement of the fishery regulations under the administration of the present minister; also to the clearing out of streams, the abolition of the saw-dust nuisance and other things which tend to improve the fishing industry in its basic principles. Other phases of action will doubtless be personally touched upon by the hon. minister before this discussion closes.
One other point that I should like to emphasize is in connection with the statistics which have been placed on ' Hansard ' to-night. I wish to point out that the administration of the Marine and Fisheries service under the present minister Is apparently bearing abundant fruit, because the returns for the year 1913 given by the hon. member for Guysborough to-night show that in that year there has been the largest increase in the output of fish for any period during the last ten years.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. F. CARROLL (South Oape Breton) :
speechtext:
I desire to say a few words in regard to the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Guysborough with reference to increased facilities for the transportation of fish to the United States. So far as I personally am concerned, I am much indebted to the hon. member for Guysborough, firstly for bringing this resolution before the House, secondly for the vast amount of information which he has given us. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. McCurdy), while he taunted members on this side of the House, who had spoken of this subject, on being bad indicators as to the way in which it should be done, resumed his geat without giving us very much light as to how it should be done. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queens should be as much interested as any member on this side of the House in getting wide markets for the Maritime provinces for the products of the sea; and if he is in a position to criticise hon. members who have spoken on their inability or incapacity to show how a better market and increased facilities could be obtained for the transportation of our fish, then he should be in a position to tell us exactly how the whole matter should be carried out. I wish to be fair with the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens, as I believe he is as much interested in this particular subject as any hon. member from the province of Nova

Scotia. I do not think, however, that he did himself justice in the way in which he approached this subject. He said that a great benefit was given to the fishing industry of the province of Nova Scotia by the killing of reciprocity, but in the same breath he told us that the free market with the United States is worth something to the [DOT]fishing industry of the province of Nova Scotia. If the United States fish market is to-day worth something to the people of Nova Scotia, it would have been worth a great deal more under reciprocity, because whereas to-day, under the Underwood tariff, we have to compete in that market with the whole world, under the reciprocity agreement we were the sole people of this world who would be allowed to send our fish into the United States market free of duty. In Newfoundland we have to compete with the greatest fishermen in the world. As -a matter of fact the people of Nova Scotia are to-day unable to compete with them. We have not got the same facilities.
We are not, however, discussing reciprocity; we are discussing a proposition which will enable the fishermen of eastern Nova Scotia to get their fish to the best market in the easiest way. So far as the county of Cape Breton is concerned, the southern portions of that county, which I have the honour to represent, is practically without railways. The fishermen along the southern shore are not in a position to send their fish to market. The hon. member for Queens P.E.I. (Mr. A. A. McLean) and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens said that we have a great market in Canada. Undoubtedly we have a great market for fish in Canada, but what we in the eastern part of Nova Scotia are concerned with is the facilities for getting our fish to market. We do not care where the market is, whether it is in the United States, in Ontario, in Quebec, or in the West.
For the past two years resolutions have been introduced for the building of branch lines in the eastern section of Nova Scotia .as feeders for the Intercolonial railway. I supported those resolutions on the ground that they would give the southern section of my constituency the opportunity of getting our farm products and the products *of the sea to market. The Government have not given these resolutions much consideration. If they have given them any *consideration, they have not told us so, and there is nothing in the Estimates to show that they are going to assist us in this respect.
The hon. member for Guysborough has put two propositions before the Government. The first is the building of branch lines as feeders of the Intercolonial railway. That would lessen the difficulties that the fishermen in his constituency have in getting their fish to market. It would also lessen the difficulties which the fishermen in southern Cape Breton have in getting their fish to market. It will take some time however, to build railways, and the Government have not started doing so yet. They have nothing in the Estimates for that purpose, and I must say that the first proposition of the hon. member for Guysborough seems to be a dead letter at the present time. Now, so far as the product of our fisheries is concerned we have only one way of getting them to market, and that is by a line of steamboats. Although I believe that at the present time the Boston market is the very best market the Nova Scotia fishermen have, yet I am not very particular where these subsidized boats carry the fish so long as they carry them to a good market.
We have in the southern section of the island of Gape Breton very good harbours. We have Louisburg, one of the very best harbours in the world, open the year round. We have a fairly good harbour at Gaba-rouse, which is one of the most important fishing stations on the north Atlantic, and another very important fishing station at Main-a-dieu. Unfortunately the harbour there is not good; but in the summer, with a line of steamers running along that shore, they could easily take their fish out and put them aboard these steamers. With reference to the question of whether we should or should not have a direct line from the eastern section of Nova Scotia- and I would call attention to the fact that my own constituency is most easterly-to the city of Boston or the New England states, that is a matter which the Government should consider. It was suggested, I think, by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that perhaps a line of steamers might be subsidized along the eastern shore of Nova Scotia which would connect with the Yarmouth line. From the statement of my hon. friend from Yarmouth I should think that the Yarmouth line as it at present exists, is over taxed, for he tells us that freight is being left on the wharfs at Yarmouth that these steamers cannot carry. It is sometimes considered very peculiar that we should be

losing population in the eastern part of Nova Scotia, and especially in the fishing and fanning districts of Cape Breton. We are sometimes told that it is the people's own fault, that they flock to the mine and steel works and industrial centres. That is not the case. The people of the district I represent, especially around Louisburg, Gabarouse and Main-a-dieu would never have to go into the mining industry or into the steel works if they had proper facilities for shipping their fish from their homes. The lack of such facilities has been a grievance with them for many years. They have the very best fishing grounds in the world along that 10 p.m. shore. And the prices are good, both in Canada and the United States. The only difficulty is in getting the fish to market. What is the good of taking fish from the sea if you are going to let them rot on the shore? As a result of the inadequacy, or I may say the absolute want, of facilities for transportation in that part of the country, the people are forced to leave their homes and go into the industrial centres. I desire to tell you, Mr. Speaker, and also the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) who is in his seat, that, in my humble estimation that is the reason why the districts along the shore of southern Nova Scotia are becoming depopulated. And I think the hon. minister could not do a better thing ror tne province of Nova Scotia, especially the southern districts, than to subsidize, tnis session, a line of steamboats which would either connect with the boats at Yarmouth or run direct from the eastern sections of Nova Scotia to New England. Now, we aTe thankful to both Governments, the present and the late Government, for anything they have done to make the transportation of our province easier. But I say they have not done enough. The port of Yarmouth, at least, has not very much to complain of. In the first place, they have a railway running into that district, and then they have a direct line of steamers to Boston. As to our part of the country- and I say this in all seriousness, I never was more serious in my life-if something is not done to help the fishermen get the products of their labour to the market, the district from Port Hawkesbury to Glace Bay will be depopulated in a short time, and I hold that the Government-any government, either this or any other-would not wish to see that; every government 
wishes to do the best it can. But if they wish to do the best they can for that section of the country, it is their bounden duty, at this session-not letting it be further postponed-to de something to subsidize a line of steamboats to that section of the country that will give an outlet to the product of the fisheries of eastern Nova Scotia.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The resolution which my
hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has moved in favour of providing better transport for fresh fish between the Maritime provinces and the United States is one that, I am sure, is worthy of very careful attention on the part of the House and of the Government. It refers more particularly to matters which come within the control of my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) and my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane), because the means of transportation which the hon. gentleman suggests are, first the construction of branch railways in the county of Guysborough and, second, the providing of steamers for the purpose of carrying the products of the fisheries to market. The hon. Minister of Railways has not been in his place this evening, but I will call his attention to the matter,-though, perhaps it is hardly necessary to do so, for on several previous occasions I have heard the hon. member for Guysborough, when the Minister of Railways and Canals was present, pointing out what a great advantage the construction of these branch lines would be, and, among the advantages he claimed was that they would afford facilities for' the shipment of the products of the fisheries. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is in his place, and it will not be necessary to call his attention to the matter further. I was sorry that the hon. member for Guysborough did not formulate some plan or tell us in what way he would sug-test that his ideas could be carried into effect. And when I interposed and asked him if he suggested that there should be a direct line of steamers from Canso or other ports along the eastern coast of Nova Scotia to the markets, or whether he would favour a line of steamers along the coast connecting with the steamers from Yarmouth to Boston, he had not his mind thoroughly made up and would not give an opinion on the subject.
I would be in favour of a direct line from Nova Scotia to Boston, if it be possible to get it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman did
not give me that information before. He rather sidestepped the question when I asked it. We have now his opinion with regard to it. While the subject for discussion to-night was the importance of affording better transportation for the fishermen in the Maritime provinces, at the same time, it seems to me that my hon. friends opposite who have discussed the question, with scarcely an exception, while I do not in any way dispute their bona fides and desire to advance the interests of the fishermen in their constituencies, seemed even more desirous o.f making political capital against the Government than of advancing the interests of the fishermen who are their constituents. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) and the hon. member for Yarmouth (Mr. Law) have harked back to the reciprocity question of September, 1911. The hon. gentlemen are very fond of telling that they accept public opinion and how desirous they are that the public should be consulted on questions, and yet, when the public are consulted on a great question like reciprocity and give an emphatic verdict on it, the hon. gentlemen are not willing to accept the verdict of the public and come here and complain about the verdict having been given against them.
I accept the verdict given in the county of Yarmouth.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friends, both of
whom represent counties where there are large fishing industries, are entirely oblivious of the fact tjiat in the county of Lunenburg, the greatest fishing county in Nova Scotia, and the county of Queen 3-Shelburne, a great fishing county with great fishing interests, the reciprocity pact was discussed from the business and trade standpoint as thoroughly as possible, because the Liberal candidate in Queens-Shelburne was a gentleman able to discuss the question probably as well as any man in Canada, he himself had been one of the originators of the pact-they entirely forget that those two great fishing counties of the province of Nova Scotia, in no uncertain term pronounced against the reciprocity pact and in favour of the policy advocated by the Conservative party in 1911. It seems to me that in view of that it is rather absurd for the hon. gentlemen to
come to this House now and say that the fishermen of Nova Scotia were in favour of reciprocity and that the reciprocity pact was in the interests of the fishermen of Nova Scotia. The hon. member for Yarmouth who has tried to introduce some politics into the discussion by referring to the condition of Yarmouth harbour, asked why are large appropriations not made for the purpose of dredging? A very substantial appropriation is being made this year. We know the condition of Yarmouth harbour, we know that when, a few years ago, the Niobe was brought from Halifax to Yarmouth at the request of the hon. gentleman and against the wishes of the responsible official of the Naval Department in order that the officers might take part in a ball given in connection with an olcf home week, it was unable to enter the harbour and a storm coming up when she was in the roadstead she put to sea, the result being of a character which cost this country $300,000 of the people's money. Let me ask my hon. friend who drags this in now simply for political purposes, where he was during the fifteen, years the Liberal party were in power that he allowed Yarmouth harbour to remain in that condition? Why did not my hon. friend, who is a very influential supporter of the Liberal (Government, try during those fifteen years to see that Yarmouth was put in the condition in which he thinks the Conservatives should put it in the two and a half years they have been in power? My hon. friend froA Inverness suggests that the harbours in Inverness county were in a deplorable condition. They have not got into a deplorable condition in two and a half years. If they were in good condition when the Conservative party came into power they would not be in a deplorable condition now, even if they were neglected. Then let me ask my hon. friend why it was that during the fifteen years the Liberal party were in power he permitted the harbours of Inverness to get into this condition, why he did not get his friends to put them into good condition in that time.

The breakwaters along our harbours at Port Hood and Margaree were destroyed owing to the storms of last year and the year before, with the knowledge of the Department of Public Works and of the engineers of the Government; and notwithstanding the fact that $200,000 had been appropriated for use in the county of Inverness, and would

have been spent in that county if the late Government had remained in power, all these wharfs were destroyed. The wharf at Port Hood, which cost $50,000, was absolutely destroyed. An appendix to a wharf was started last year under the supervision of my hon. friend. That new structure has been carried away, with the knowledge of the Government, and they never spent even a dollar to preserve the property of the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
As I understand storms
came last year which carried away wharfs and breakwaters.
And the year before.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
One would almost imagine [DOT]that the hon., gentleman held the Government responsible for having brought these storms and that the damage which resulted from the storms last year and the year before should have been repaired by this time. A moment's reflection will show the hon. gentleman how weak his argument is in that respect.
I was referring to the fact that hon. gentlemen, in discussing this question, were unable to get away from political considerations, and were dealing with it in a way to make political capital. I come down, however, to a consideration of the facts. My hon. friend from Inverness (Mr. Chisholm) said he would like to give credit to the late Government for what they have done in the way of developing trade in fish between Nova Scotia and the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. I would not for one moment detract in the slightest possible degree from any credit that might be due the Government which my hon. friend supports or anything they did in connection with the development of that industry. They arranged that fish should be taken [DOT] by fast freight in fast freight cars. That was good as far as it went, and the present -Government has taken a step far more in the public interest and a great step in advance by arranging for the fish to be taken from the Maritime provinces, in the last twelve months, in refrigerator express *cars, with results most beneficial to the .fishermen of the Maritime provinces in ^enabling them to get fish on the markets * of Ontario and the West in a very much better condition.

I would like to understand exactly the difference between the [plan adopted by the present Government 
and that put in force by the late Government for the carrying of these fish.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Under the arrangement
made by the late Administration the fish went forward by fast freight. That ' was continued, but there was an arrangement
made by which fish now goes forward by express cars.

I think the minister
will find that it went forward by express before-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: -going more rapidly, going under better circumstances and delivered on the market in better condition than previously.

How do trains go more rapidly than under the old system? The arrangement made by the late Government provided not only for fish going forward by express cars, but for payment of one-third of the express charges, which the present Government is also doing. I want the minister to point out the difference between the plan of the former Government and the present Government in regard to express cars.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is not the slightest trouble in showing the difference. Now a cold storage express refrigerator car is sent forward every Saturday attached to an express train and the Government guarantees that that car will contain a certain number of pounds of fish; if it does not contain that much the Government will pay for the deficiency, and that has proved such a very great success that in many cases there is no deficiency to be paid for at all, and we believe it will be practically self-supporting and will be no burden on the country.
Did not the late Government provide express cars?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The guarantee under the former Government was for fast freight cars not attached to express trains, and cars, not running every day, but only two or three times a week. We have provided for this car, attached to an express train, to run every Saturday.
My hon. friend from Guysborough referred to the report of the Marine and Fisheries Department this year and made some quotations. The hon. gentleman approved of what was being done by the department in regard to having fish placed on the markets of the upper provinces. I may say that the movement inaugurated by my

predecessor in office, and carried on with extensions and improvements since, has proved a great success. There has been an increasing amount of fish going forward, and at one-third of the charges prevailing under the arrangement made by the late Government. I do not want to take up the time of this House or bore it in any way, but my hon. friend from Guysborough has referred very properly to the report of the Marine and Fisheries Department, and I think it is only proper that I should place on 'Hansard' an extract from that report covering the part of the extract referred to by my hon. friend. On page 15, hon. gentlemen will find under the heading, transportation of fresh and mildly cured fish, the following statement:
The department's policy in aiding- in the stimulation and development of the trade in fresh and mildly cured fish in the interior portions of the country, by placing at the disposal of the shippers cheap rates and additional facilities and equipment, is having most gratifying results.
Prior to the time that the department undertook to assist, such markets as those in Montreal and Toronto were being very largely supplied from United States sources. The Canadian business was so small that the railways did not find it feasible to place cold storage cars, which would be hauled by fast freight, at the disposal of the shippers and the express rates were so high that successful competition with United States shippers was not found possible. This will be realized from the following: The express rate on fish from Halifax and Mulgrave is $1.50 per 100 pounds, while from Portland the rate is but 80 cents. As, however, there is an import duty of 1 cent per pound the gross rate is $1.80. The advantage of 30 cents per 100 pounds to the Canadian shipper was more than offset by the fact that at United States ports, owing to the very large number of vessels operating therefrom, a supply of fish could always be relied upon, and as the haul is short, orders could be sent up to within a few hours before the consignments were needed. Along the Canadian coast the demand for fresh fish was comparatively small and uncertain. Hence no great effort was being made by the fishermen to land fish during unfavourable weather, so that dealers could not rely on having their orders filled exactly when required, which is an absolute necessity In the carrying on of a successful business in the sale of fish.
To overcome these disadvantages and to assure, not only the Canadian market being supplied from Canadian sources, but a rapid expansion of such markets as well, the department took up the question of procuring better rates and shipping facilities. The railway and express companies did not, however, see their way clear to do more than they were doing, keeping in view the volume of the business that seemed available. The department, therefore, arranged to have the railway place at the disposal of the shippers a cold storage car on two days each week, which car would be hauled by fast freight to Montreal. To enable this to be done the department guaranteed that the earnings on these cars would be at least two-thirds those on a minimum carload lot of 20,000 pounds, at carload lot rates from the point of starting to destination, plus $4 per car for icing.
This service has proved a great boon to the trade. While it cost the department a considerable amount annually for the first few years, it is now being taken advantage of to such an extent that it is practically self-sustaining.
While a cold storage freight service is efficient for the supplying of a substantial market, such as that of Fridays, it soon became apparent that if a considerable demand for fish on other days were to be worked up, express facilities at reasonable rates must be available to the shippers.
This was done about a year ago, if my recollection is correct.
The department consequently arranged with the express companies to accept responsibility for one-third of the ordinary express rates on all shipments of fresh and mildly cured fish including shell-fish, from the Atlantic coast as far west as the eastern boundary of Manitoba, and from the Pacific coast as far east as the said boundary. This gave the shippers from Halifax or Mulgrave a rate of $1 per 100 lbs. to Montreal, and proportionately from intervening points, or an advantage to the Canadian coast dealers of at least 80 cents per 100 lbs. over the United States shipper.
With such facilities and rates the Canadian dealers did not take long to demonstrate that they could control the situation. Not only has the importation of fresh fish along the Canadian Atlantic coast been stopped from the United States, but the demand in the Canadian markets is being very rapidly expanded.
While the dealers on the Pacific coast have for several years been sending fish through to Toronto and Montreal in carload lots, on which they are given a rate of $3 per 100 lbs., the express charges in less than carload lots to the prairie provinces were so high that the working up of any large trade there seemed out of the question. The rate from Vancouver or New Westminster to Calgary is $3.50 per 100 lbs., and to Edmonton, Qu'Appelle or Winnipeg $4.50 per 100 lbs.
With the cheaper rate given owing to the departmental assistance the trade has increased wonderfully and now shipments are being sent in carload lots to quite an extent making departmental assistance unnecessary.
Then follow the .figures showing how the business from the East and West by express alone has been expanding. It is evident from the facts as they present themselves, that the department has not been at all lacking in its desire to develop the fish trade between Nova Scotia points and points in Ontario and Quebec. A further arrangement was entered into last year with the express companies and the Intercolonial railway, whereby a cold storage express car for the transportation of fish leaves Mulgrave for Montreal on Saturday of each week. Shipments for Halifax are consolidated in this car at Truro. It arrives in Montreal on Sunday night in

time to connect with the Toronto train, so that the shipments for Toronto reach there by ordinary express cars Monday morning -leaving Mulgrave on Saturday, the fish are ready for delivery in Toronto on Monday morning. In addition to that, I may say that the Fisheries Department during the year had an exhibit at the Toronto Exhibition-the first exhibit of our fisheries that was ever made there which attracted a great deal of attention, and which, in the belief of many dealers, has done a great deal to develop the business in the markets of Ontario, and of the lower provinces, and has been the cause of larger orders being given in the Maritime provinces. There has been some controversy here to-night over the Advisory Board, and I am glad to find that the general opinion of hon. gentlemen is in favour of the constitution of that Board, and that their belief is that it will be of benefit so far as the development of the fisheries of Canada is concerned. The only criticism that has been made is in regard to its personnel. My hon. friend from Inverness (Mr. Chisholm) has suggested that some member from that county should be appointed to the Board. I am sorry I cannot comply with his request, much as I would like to. There are four members on the Board from Nova Scotia at present, and while no doubt there is not a part of Nova Scotia interested in fishing that would not like to have a representative on the Board, I am quite sure my hon. friend will see how impossible it is to have every county represented. The four representatives from Nova Scotia, I believe, are gentlemen well qualified to deal with the question. There is a gentleman from Lunenburg, Mr. Smith, who thoroughly understands deep-sea fishing; Mr. Gideon A. Hemeon, of Queens and Sheldon, a practical fisherman; Mr. Short from Digby, who is thoroughly au fait with this question. Then there is a gentleman from Halifax, appointed on the recommendation of the Board of Trade of that, city, who has a special knowledge of the salt fish and dried fish industry, which centre very largely in the city of Halifax.
From St. Andrews, New Brunswick, on Passamaquoddy Bay, we have Mr. Bussell, a gentleman who is a practical fisherman himself and a fish dealer. We have a gentleman from Kent county, and we have Mr. Young from Gloucester county. Mr. Young has been in the fish business all his life, is in touch with the fishermen and he was appointed to the Advisory Board at the

request of the fishermen and those interested in the fishing industry. We have a gentleman from the Gaspe coast and these gentlemen I have named, four from Nova Scotia, four from New Brunswick, one from the Gaspe coast and one from Prince Edward Island, Mr. Longworth, constitute the eastern section of the Advisory Fisheries Board. I think it would be a very difficult matter to find any number of gentlemen with a more thorough or intimate knowledge of the fisheries of the Maritime provinces than that possessed by these gentlemen. I am glad to be able to assure this House that the permanent officers of the Fisheries Department are of the opinion that this board as constituted is of most valuable assistance in the development of the fisheries of this country and one which can give sound advice as to the line along which we should proceed and the methods which should be adopted in the development of the fisheries and of the fishing trade.
One word more about some remarks made by the hon. member for Guysborough. He referred to the subsidy granted to the West Indian line of steamships and the subsidy granted by the country to the line of steamships sailing to South Africa. It seems to me that the subsidy granted to the West Indian line of steamships is one that is very much in the interest of the fishing industry of the lower provinces, because a great deal of the freight that is carried by the West Indian line of steamships is fish exported from Halifax to the West Indies who are large consumers of fish oaught in Nova Scotia waters, cured and dried there and sent to the consumers of the West Indies. I am sure that the hon. member for Guysborough and other hon. gentlemen from Nova Scotia, knowing the importance of that service, would be among the last to suggest that the money is not properly expended or that the service is not a proper one in the public interest.
I did not make any such suggestions.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I did not say you did.
I simply referred to the fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I referred to the fact and I said that I believed that my hon. friend would be the last one to suggest the stopping of this service altogether.

I did not suggest anything of the kind.

Mr. nAZEN: What was the purpose ot my hon. friend in referring to it at all?

I made the statement that if the Government would give half of the amount that it was giving for the expansion of trade in South Africa and in South America, we would get better results from the trade between the Maritime provinces and the United States in connection with the fresh fish trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Am I to understand that the hon. gentleman suggests a reduction of one-half of the subsidy given by the Government to this West Indian service?
Mr. -SINCLAIR: Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman referred to it for one purpose only, and that was that he wanted to create the impression in Nova Scotia that the Government had plenty of money to give to a service which was not very useful to the country, not nearly so useful as the one he advocated, and the subsidy which he tried to make it appear was not very useful was the subsidy granted to the West Indian steamship line. I am pointing out that this subsidy is of very great value to the fishing industry of Nova Scotia, because I think that I am correct in saying that the bulk of the freight that is carried by the West Indian steamships down to the West Indies is composed of fish caught and cured in Nova Scotia and sent down to the market of the West Indies.
As far as the South African service is concerned, perhaps I might point out that, whereas a few years ago we were sending comparatively small quantities of products to South Africa, owing to the steamship service, I find by the Trade and Navigation returns that last year we sent to South Africa $3,340,513 worth of Canadian products. They went, I think, practically altogether by this subsidized line of steamers, managed by the Elder Dempster Company, and sailing from Montreal in summer and from a Maritime province port in winter to South Africa. The business has been a growing one, and it will continue to grow. This export is made up largely of flour, agricultural implements, newspaper print and other products of Canadian workshops and farms, and that this subsidy is having good results is shown in the development of the trade of Canada and in the opening up of such markets for our manufacturers and producers of other sorts.
The Department of Marine and Fisheries has not -been idle in regard to improvement in the matter of the transportation of fresh fish between the Maritime provinces and the United States. The question has been receiving the consideration of myself and the permanent officers of the department during the past two seasons. By my direction and at my request last year an officer of the department interviewed the officers of the company operating the steamship service between Yarmouth and Boston and arrangements were then made by which the steamship company undertook the more careful and expeditious handling of fresh fish in transit between the Maritime provinces and Boston. Complaints reached the department similar to those made by one hon. gentleman here to-night, complaints that I think were well founded, that lobsters especially were being very carelessly handled, with the result that they reached the Boston market sometimes in a condition which seriously impaired their value. We had the matter investigated. We had an official of the department go down to Boston and be present at the landing of these boats and see the condition in which the fish were, and I am advised by the Deputy M in-ister and other officers in the department that the improvements that have been made have to a very considerable extent been carried out by the steamship companies, that a great deal more care in the handling of fish has been exercised, with the result that fresh lobsters are now in a much more marketable condition when they arrive in the Boston market than they were previously to these inquiries and investigations being made. I am advised by the officials of the department that as a result of the representations made arrangements have been made for more prompt deliveries at Boston on the arrival of the various steamers from Maritime province ports and that better transportation facilities are being provided. At the opening of the present fishing season I directed attention to the matter and requested that the officers of the department should give their consideration to it with the view of bringing about some further improvements. The Superintendent of Fisheries went carefully into the subject, and he has submitted a memorandum pointing out the different steps which should oe taken in order to bring about the desired improvements. These improvements involve negotiations with the Department of Trade and Commerce apd these are in progress at the present time. The steamship

line which has been referred to as running between Yarmouth and Boston operates one boat from the first of October to the first of June, making two trips a week. After that two boats are put on, which make four trips a week up to the end of July. Then a third boat is put on to the end of October. So that from the first of June to the end of October the service out of Yarmouth is a daily service. There havd been recent negotiations with the company and we hope that a second boat will be placed on the route from October to June instead of one boat as at present. There has been a very large expansion of the shipping business from Yarmouth during recent months and it is to be hoped that with that large expansion of business the steamship company will find that it will be possible to put on a daily service during the months that I have mentioned in order to carry this trade to Boston, and which, as I understand, has been fairly profitable to the company looking at it from a purely business standpoint. The other suggestion, that these boats run along the coast, connecting with the Yarmouth boats, does not find special favour with my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair), who thinks a direct service would be better. But all these questions will have to be considered by the Department of Trade and Commerce.
I think I am absolutely correct in saying that for a period of 15 years, no subsidy has been voted by the Parliament of Canada for a line of steamers running from a Canadian port to a port in the United States, and that is a matter which is worth remembering in connection with this whole question. No subsidy has been given to the line of steamers running from St. John to Portland and Boston, or to the line running from Yarmouth to Boston and return, or from Halifax to Boston and return. However, with the extensive business consequent on the increased development of our fisheries, it would seem to me that the company itself might find it in its own interest, without any subsidy from the Dominion Parliament to put on a line of steamers running daily during the fishing season or during the season when business is most active, between Yarmouth and ports in the United States, as steamers run daily during a great part of the season between St. John and Boston.
I	agree with the hon. member for Guys-borough as to the possibility of developing the fishing industry of Canada. Up to a few years ago Nova Scotia was the premier fish-producing province of Canada. To-day, British Columbia is enormously pro-

ductive. The northern waters of that province are teeming with fish, and although up to the present the industry has been largely developed in only two varieties, the halibut and the salmon, the waters of British Columbia are filled with herring, and sole, and crabs, and other fish, the trade in which can be developed to enormous proportions. With the opening of the Grand Trunk Pacific from Prince Rupert to the East, I believe, from my own personal knowledge and observation in northern British Columbia this year, that in a few years Prince Rupert will not only be the greatest fish port on the continent of America, but probably the greatest fish port in the world. In addition to our fisheries on the eastern and western coasts, we have splendid fisheries in the immense inland lakes, where the industry is capable of great development, with resultant increase in the wealth of the country, and an added source of food supply for the people of the prairie provinces. Owing to the wanton destruction of fish in the past, we will have1 to take measures to repair the mischief that has been done, by providing for file artificial production of the fish. To a very considerable extent, measures in that direction are being taken to-day. This Parliament annually votes a large sum of money for the erection of fish hatcheries and for the maintenance of those already in existence. The Superintendent of Fisheries informs me that for the first time since we have established' fish hatcheries in Canada, they are to-day filled with eggs and are being more successfully operated now than at any time in the past. It has been demonstrated that the salmon hatcheries have done most useful work. The fishermen along the coast of St. John county, who drift out almost across to the Nova Scotia shore night after night in the prosecution of their calling, tell me that there now is no such thing as a year when they are not getting a good supply of salmon. These salmon come up the bay of Fundy, and along the coast making for the spawning grounds on the St. John and Tobique rivers, and they are being caught at points along that river where they were not caught at 15 or 20 years ago, and they are being caught in great numbers. That is a very desirable state of things, and it is due to the more perfect enforcement of the fishery laws, and due most of all to the work of the salmon hatcheries. The same thing is true as to the whitefish hatcheries on the Great Lakes, and although the results obtained from the lobster hatcheries may at the present time

be a matter of some doubt, I trust that in a few years the utility of these hatcheries will be fully demonstrated and that they may in time to come make up for the past depletion of the lobsters fisheries. I entirely agree with one hon. gentleman opposite who said that there has not been as much done for the fisheries of Canada by the Department of Marine and Fisheries as should have been done, but I can assure my hon. friend that the officials of the department to-day are doing their very utmost to promote and develop the fishing industry, and for my part I am giving them the very best assistance and support that it is within my power to give. I trust that in years to come good results will flow from the efforts now being made by the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Now that my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has brought this matter before the House, and has had a full discussion of it, which will no doubt be of benefit, as is every discussion concerning the development of our great national ressouroes, I presume he will consent to the usual course of adjourning the debate.
On motion of Mr. Hazen, the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Rogers, the House adjourned at 10.45 p.m.
Tuesday, February 3, 1914.
